name: Post-war consensus
summary: The post-war consensus is the shared acceptance, by Britain's main parties from 1945 to the late 1970s, of a mixed economy, Keynesian demand management aimed at high employment, an extensive welfare state including the NHS, and conciliation of the trade unions. It was reached by Labour revisionists and middle-way Conservatives who preferred piecemeal, empirical change to doctrine and class conflict. Historians dispute how real the consensus was, and the parties differed over nationalisation and equality.

scope: The British post-war consensus of 1945 to the late 1970s as Williams, Blackburn, Dorey and Britannica (under its name Butskellism) describe it: the Labour revisionist and Conservative one-nation common ground on the mixed economy, full employment, the welfare state, trade-union conciliation and piecemeal change. Its own texts are the Conservative Industrial Charter (1947) as quoted by Williams. The New Zealand use of the term, the global "embedded liberalism" sense, Thatcherism and One Nation Conservatism beyond the consensus years are excluded.

aliases.name: Butskellism
aliases.quote: Often referred to as the post-war consensus, commitments would include accepting the mixed economy, the advocacy of industrial partnership, social reform and achieving full employment. Although the degree of consensus is disputed within the existing literature, (a debate neatly summed up by Blackburn) 31 , the Conservative governments of 1951-64 would utilize these concepts in their approach to economic, industrial relations and trade union policy. This approach was satirically labelled as Butskellism

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Beveridge makes compulsory state social insurance with a national minimum the core of the plan and leaves voluntary action only as a supplement above it.

class-collaboration.rationale: Britannica defines the Butskellism consensus as resting on collaboration between social classes, and the Charter and its follow-up ask management and labour to work in partnership rather than as permanent opposites.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The 1947 Industrial Charter, which Williams presents as the basis of the consensus, says the aim of national policy should be a basic standard of living and security of outlook for all people; the Beveridge Report likewise sets a national minimum guaranteeing freedom from want.

gradual-change.rationale: Blackburn finds that Labour revisionists and middle-way Conservatives agreed piecemeal change was preferable to radical change, which kept their disagreements inside one set of limits.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Beveridge makes compulsory state social insurance, paying pensions as of right from a fund built on current contributions, the method of the plan, with voluntary insurance only as a subsidiary.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Addison, as Heffernan reports him, found ministers of both parties borne along by a belief in the state as a modernising instrument, and the consensus package of full employment, the NHS and social insurance rests on an active state.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Williams says One Nation Conservatives justified their consensus approach by a sense of noblesse oblige: privilege carried a corresponding duty of public service.

public-ownership.rationale: The record points both ways: the Conservative governments left coal, rail and the Bank of England nationalised yet denationalised iron and steel (1953) and road haulage (1954).

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The 1951-64 Conservative governments shelved their pledge to repeal Labour's Trade Disputes Act and, fearing to antagonise the unions, chose not to legislate against strikes even when pressed to.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The Charter opposes a rigid straitjacket of doctrinaire theory laid on the nation regardless of economic facts, and Williams lists eschewing ideology as a theme of the consensus Conservatism.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Beveridge builds a universal contributory scheme covering all citizens without a means test, while the consensus Conservatives held that help should go first to those in need, so its own sources split.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Williams records that the 1951-64 Conservative governments left the NHS largely untouched and kept their commitment to it, continuing the health service Labour created.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Dorey says industrial partnership explicitly did not mean employees would hold equal authority or power with employers; it meant communication and consultation, not a worker vote.

missingStatements.text: Governments should be responsible for keeping unemployment low.
missingStatements.rationale: Maintaining high employment is a founding commitment of the consensus: Beveridge assumes avoidance of mass unemployment, and the Conservative Industrial Charter holds future governments responsible for a high and stable level of employment.

notes: Searched themes: economy (nationalisation, planning, employment, welfare, health, housing), industrial relations, means. Foreign policy, empire, defence and constitutional themes (government, culture, ecology, technology) are not covered by the defining sources available (Kavanagh and Morris, Crosland and the full Beveridge Report could not be opened), so those stay null. Wikipedia only guided the search. Dorey and Williams write about One Nation Conservatism, the Conservative strand of the consensus; their account of the Charter counts only as far as Williams ties it to the consensus.
